events.description: Gen. Petraeus says al-Qaeda no longer operating in Afghanistan.
Gen. James Jones claims fewer than 100 al-Qaeda operatives in Afghanistan.
U.S. intelligence and DoD officials tell ABC News al-Qaeda has about 100 operatives in Afghanistan.
Blogger Michael Yon claims no al-Qaeda being killed or captured.
CIA Director Panetta gives the '50 to 100' al-Qaeda estimate in Afghanistan (hosts say June/July 2010).
ISAF announces death of al-Qaeda associate Sabar Lal Melma; press release discloses 40+ al-Qaeda killed in eastern Afghanistan Jan-Jul 2011.
Ilyas Kashmiri killed in U.S. drone strike (hosts unsure: 2009-2011).
ISAF stops issuing press releases on raids against al-Qaeda.
Roggio and Patrick Meegan map ISAF raids: 338 raids in 25 of 34 provinces, 110 districts.
Four-day joint U.S.-Afghan raid on al-Qaeda training camps in Shorabak, including one of ~30 square miles; 150-200 al-Qaeda killed or captured.
Nicholson's team says 50 al-Qaeda leaders and 200 AQIS members taken off battlefield in 2016.
Pompeo says fewer than 200 al-Qaeda in Afghanistan, a couple days after 9/11 anniversary.

key_claims: The U.S. estimate of fewer than 200 al-Qaeda in Afghanistan is not credible and is meant to justify withdrawal.
The 50-100 estimate was 'sticky' from 2010 to early 2016, ignoring raid data such as ISAF press releases and the Shorabak camps.
Al-Qaeda deliberately operates clandestinely under the Islamic Emirate banner and rarely advertises operations, now often in Urdu/Pashto.
AQIS, TIP, TTP and other allied groups by themselves likely exceed 200 in Afghanistan, and AQIS is fully part of al-Qaeda.
Al-Qaeda has dual-hatted figures such as Qari Zia Rahman and Aminullah Peshwari, which complicates counting.
The Afghanistan-Pakistan border is fluid, and al-Qaeda also uses Balochistan and Karachi, not just Waziristan.
The Taliban deny any al-Qaeda presence, which undermines the idea they will turn on al-Qaeda.
